subject: Culture
title: Valentine's Day Commerce
description: A short lesson to help you apply Valentine's Day Commerce.

hook.text: Valentine's Day generates $26 billion in US spending annually. The saint it's named for was beheaded.

buildup.text: Saint Valentine was a Roman martyr. His link to romance didn't appear until Chaucer wrote about it in 1382.

discovery.text: Hallmark began mass-producing Valentine's cards in 1913. The industry created the modern holiday.

twist.text: Japan flipped it: women give chocolate to men on February 14th. Men return the favor on White Day, March 14th.

climax.text: Valentine's Day proves that commerce can build a tradition from almost nothing in a few decades.

punchline.text: Love is real. The holiday was manufactured.

quiz.question: When did Hallmark begin mass-producing Valentine's Day cards?

details.summary: Valentine's Day transformed from a medieval saint's feast into a $26 billion commercial industry. Greeting card companies, chocolate makers, and diamond sellers manufactured romantic obligation into one of the most commercially successful holidays ever created — largely from the 20th century onward.
details.whyItMatters: Valentine's Day is a case study in how commerce manufactures emotional obligation. Understanding its commercial construction helps consumers recognize similar manufactured holidays.
takeaways: Valentine's Day generates over $26 billion in US spending annually
The diamond engagement ring was invented by a De Beers ad campaign

faq.question: How did Valentine's Day become commercialized?
faq.answer: Pre-printed valentines appeared in the 1840s. Cadbury created heart-shaped chocolate boxes in 1861. Hallmark began mass-producing valentines in 1913. Each generation of marketers added new 'traditions' — roses, jewelry, expensive dinners.

faq.question: Who was Saint Valentine?
faq.answer: At least three different Saint Valentines are recognized by the Catholic Church, and their stories are largely legendary. The most popular story — a priest who secretly married soldiers — has no historical verification. Geoffrey Chaucer first linked Valentine's Day to romance in 1375.
